content: Liver cancer is a condition where cells in the liver grow uncontrollably. The liver is located in the upper abdomen, near the stomach, intestines, gallbladder, and pancreas. It performs several critical functions, including storing nutrients, removing waste products and old cells from the blood, filtering and processing chemicals from food, alcohol, and medications, and producing bile, which aids in fat digestion and waste elimination. The liver also contains intrahepatic bile ducts, which are small tubes that transport bile within the liver. In the early stages, liver cancer may not present noticeable symptoms. However, as the disease progresses, individuals may experience discomfort in the upper right abdomen, a swollen abdomen, or a hard lump on the right side just below the rib cage. Pain may also occur near the right shoulder blade or in the back. Other symptoms include jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), easy bruising or bleeding, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and unexplained weight loss. It is important to note that these symptoms can also be caused by other medical conditions, so consulting a doctor is essential if they occur. Certain behaviors and conditions increase the risk of developing liver cancer. These include being overweight or obese, having chronic hepatitis B or hepatitis C infections, smoking cigarettes, consuming excessive amounts of alcohol, and having cirrhosis (liver scarring caused by hepatitis or alcohol use). Other risk factors include nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, diabetes, hemochromatosis (a condition where the body absorbs and stores excessive iron), and consuming foods contaminated with aflatoxins (toxins produced by fungi on improperly stored grains and nuts). To reduce the risk of liver cancer, individuals can take several preventive measures. Maintaining a healthy weight and engaging in regular physical activity are important. Vaccination against hepatitis B and testing for hepatitis C are also recommended, with appropriate medical care if hepatitis C is detected. Avoiding smoking or quitting if one smokes, as well as limiting alcohol consumption, can further lower the risk. The CDC provides tools to explore liver cancer statistics, including data on new cases, deaths, and trends over time. These statistics are broken down by age, sex, race, and ethnicity, and are available for the entire United States and individual states. Additionally, comprehensive cancer control programs, such as those funded by the National Comprehensive Cancer Control Program (NCCCP), focus on liver cancer prevention. For example, projects have been implemented to raise awareness about the link between injecting drugs and the risk of hepatitis and liver cancer. Educational materials have also been developed to promote hepatitis B and C screening and vaccination.
